en: *Abhidharmāvatāra-śāstra*, Fascicle One.
Composed by the Arhat Saṅghabhadra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
I pay homage to the All-Knowing One, the stainless wheel of the Buddha-sun,
whose light of speech destroys the darkness of the fundamental minds of humans, devas, and those in the evil realms.
By means of the principles of Abhidharma, he uproots the ignorance regarding the characteristics of phenomena.
I prostrate to such a treasury of the words of the All-Knowing One.
The darkness of false speech arising from inferior intellect obscures the words of the Muni;
it is through the bright lamp that they are illuminated—homage to the one who kindles that lamp.

There are those of keen intelligence who are able to fully receive and uphold both the words and meanings of the teachings of all the Munis, yet they may still fall away from what they have not yet attained due to being preoccupied with worldly affairs.

There are also those of inferior intelligence who, upon hearing the dense forest of names and meanings within the Abhidharma, give rise to fear; nevertheless, both groups constantly possess the desire to seek understanding. Therefore, wishing to cause them to joyfully and easily enter the deep, swirling depths of the ocean of dharmalakṣaṇas in the Abhidharma, this treatise is composed.
That is to say, the system of the Sugata consists of eight categories:
first, form; second, sensation; [and so forth].
3. Perception;
4. Volitional formations;
5. Consciousness;
Sixth, space; seventh, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
eighth, cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). These collectively encompass all categories of meaning.
Form is of two kinds: namely, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived form (*upādāyarūpa*).
There are four primary elements: namely, earth, water, fire, and wind.
Because the elements (*dhātu*) are able to maintain their own and common characteristics, or the various types of derived form, they are called "elements."

These four great elements (mahābhūta), in their respective order, have solidity, moisture, heat, and motion as their intrinsic natures (svabhāva); they have supporting, cohesion, maturation, and growth as their functions (karman). Because they are both "great" and "elements," they are called the great elements.

For this reason, space is not included among the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), because the meaning of "element" is that which can produce its own result; furthermore, it is called "great" because it pervades all derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
Thus, there are only four such primary elements, for there would be no further purpose or capacity [for more], just as a bed has only four legs.
Derived matter consists of eleven kinds:
first, the eye;
second, the ear;
3. Nose; 4. Tongue; 5. Body;
Sixth, visible forms;
seventh, sounds;
eighth, odors;
9. Taste; 10. a portion of tangibles;
11. non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa).
Because it exists within the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), it is called "derived" (*upādāya*); this means that it arises depending upon the primary elements.
Herein, "eye" refers to the basis of visual consciousness; its function is to see visible forms, and its essence is translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*).
The ear, nose, tongue, and body should be explained accordingly.
Form is of two kinds: namely, color (varṇa) and shape (saṃsthāna).
As the Blessed One said:
It manifests as unwholesome and takes on unwholesome forms.
Within this, there are twelve kinds of manifest color (*varṇa*), namely: blue, yellow, red, white, smoke, clouds, dust, mist, shadow, glare, light, and darkness.
There are eight kinds of shape and color, namely: long, short, square, round, high, low, regular, and irregular.
Among these, "mist" refers to the vapor of earth and water.
The flame of the sun is called "light" (*āloka*).
The flames of the moon, stars, fire, medicinal herbs, jewels, lightning, and so forth are called "clarity" (*ābhāsa*).
Obstructions arise therein, obstructing the production of light.
Other visible forms are called "shadow"; the opposite of this is called "darkness.
"Square" refers to a rectangular shape;
"round" refers to a circular shape.
Equality of shape is called "regular";
inequality of shape is called "irregular.
Other forms are easy to understand, and therefore they are not explained here.
These twenty kinds are all objects cognized by visual consciousness and the mental consciousness induced by it.
Sound is of two kinds: namely, appropriated and non-appropriated.
Because there is a distinction in their causes—the great elements—those that fall within one's own body are called "appropriated," which has the meaning of being possessed of sensation;
those contrary to this are called "unappropriated."
Those produced by the former are said to have appropriated great elements (*mahābhūta*) as their cause, namely sounds such as those of speech, hands, and so forth.
Those produced by the latter are said to have non-appropriated great elements as their cause, namely sounds such as those of wind and forests.

These are distinguished into four categories: names of sentient beings and names of non-sentient beings. Specifically, among the former sounds, vocal sounds are called "names of sentient beings," while all other sounds are called "names of non-sentient beings.
Among the latter sounds, transformed speech is called "names of sentient beings," while all other sounds are called "names of non-sentient beings."
These, moreover, are further divided into the agreeable and the disagreeable, thus forming eight types.
All eight of these are objects cognized by the ear-consciousness and the mental consciousness induced by it.
There are three kinds of fragrance:
first, pleasant fragrance; second, unpleasant fragrance;
and third, neutral fragrance.
Third, equal fragrance (*sama-gandha*).
That which can nourish the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) is called pleasant fragrance;
that which can impair the sense faculties and the primary elements is called unpleasant fragrance.
If it possesses characteristics contrary to both [sweet and bitter], it is called an "equal" fragrance (*sama-gandha*).
These three types are all objects cognized by olfactory consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñāna*) and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) induced by it.
There are six kinds of taste (*rasa*), distinguished as sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and bland.
These six kinds are all objects cognized by the tongue-consciousness and the mental consciousness induced by it.
A portion of tangibility consists of seven kinds, namely: smoothness, roughness, heaviness, lightness, as well as cold, hunger, and thirst.
Softness is called "smoothness," which is the meaning of mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśa*).
Coarseness and rigidity are called "roughness.
That which can be weighed is called "heavy"; the opposite of this is called "light."

Because they are induced by these [afflictions], the cause for the desire for warmth is called "cold," the cause for the desire for food is called "hunger," and the cause for the desire for drink is called "thirst.
These are all instances of applying the name of the effect to the cause; therefore, it is stated thus, just as it is said that "the appearance of the Buddhas is bliss," and so forth.
Within the aggregation of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), because water and fire predominate, there is the quality of smoothness;
because earth and wind predominate, there is the quality of roughness;
and because earth and water predominate, there is the quality of heaviness.
Lightness arises from the predominance of fire and wind;
coldness arises from the predominance of water and wind;
hunger arises from the predominance of wind.
Because fire increases, there is thirst.

As for non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*), it is so called because it can manifest the specific transformations of the mind and mental factors; therefore, it is termed "informative" (*vijñapti*).
Because it is of the same category as that [manifest action] yet cannot manifest it, it is called "non-manifest" (*avijñapti*).
This is an instance of applying a term of negation to something similar, just as one might say "non-Brahmin" with respect to a Kṣatriya or others.

The characteristic of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is as follows: it refers to a continuity of wholesome or unwholesome material form that arises through the differentiation of informative action, mind, and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

It persists even during sleep, wakefulness, distracted or undistracted states of mind, and even in the state of mindlessness; it cannot be accumulated, yet it serves as the basis for establishing one as a bhikṣu and so forth—this is the characteristic of non-informative matter.
If this did not exist, one could not establish the existence of bhikṣus and so forth.
As the Blessed One said: "Regarding meritorious actions based on existing things, their merit constantly increases."
Thus, there are three types of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) in total, namely: those comprised within restraint (*saṃvara*), non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), and that which is neither.
There are three types of restraint, namely: the prātimokṣa, dhyāna, and untainted (*anāsrava*) restraints, according to their specific distinctions.
Furthermore, there are eight types of prātimokṣa restraint:
first, the bhikṣu restraint;
second, the bhikṣuṇī restraint; [and so forth].
3. The śrāmaṇera-vinaya;
4. the śikṣamāṇā-vinaya; 5. the śrāmaṇerī-vinaya;
Sixth, the discipline of the male lay follower (upāsaka-vinaya);
seventh, the discipline of the female lay follower (upāsikā-vinaya);
eighth, the discipline of temporary abstinence (upavāsa-vinaya).
These eight types are associated exclusively with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

As for the *dhyāna-saṃvara* (meditative restraint), it refers to the matter that arises concomitantly with the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of the form realm; this is associated exclusively with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) refers to the matter (*rūpa*) that arises concomitantly with the untainted meditative absorption (*anāsrava-samādhi*);

this is exclusively unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*). Regarding non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), it refers to those such as butchers, hunters, bird-catchers, fishermen, robbers, prison wardens, those who bind dragons, those who cook dogs, snarers, trappers, and executioners.
Within these bodies, there proceeds a continuity of unwholesome non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) that is neither restraint (*saṃvara*) nor non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).

This refers to the various wholesome and unwholesome non-informative matters that arise and proceed as a continuity from such acts as constructing monasteries (*vihāra*), stūpas (*stūpa*), and *saṃghārāmas*; as well as prostrating before caityas, burning incense, scattering flowers, chanting praises, making vows, and even striking others with a rod.
There are also instances where non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) lasts for only a single moment; however, it is described as a "continuum" based on its general category.
The Prātimokṣa restraint is acquired through a formal vow: the first seven types last until the end of one's life, while the eighth lasts for one day and night.
Furthermore, regarding the first seven types [of vows], their relinquishment occurs due to four conditions:
first, by abandoning that which was to be studied;
second, by the end of one's life; [the remaining two conditions follow].
Third, because the roots of goodness are severed;
fourth, because of the arising of both sexual organs.
The eighth restraint is relinquished by the aforementioned four causes as well as the passing of the night.

The dhyāna restraint (dhyāna-saṃvara) is acquired through the attainment of a wholesome mind of the form realm and is relinquished through the abandonment of that wholesome mind of the form realm, because it is contingent upon that mind.
The same applies to the acquisition and relinquishment of the untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara), as it is acquired and relinquished in accordance with the untainted mind.
Non-restraint is acquired through action and through formal undertaking; it is relinquished due to four conditions:
first, by undertaking restraint;
second, by the exhaustion of one's life-span; [and so forth].
Third, because of the arising of both sexual organs;
fourth, by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), one obtains the wholesome mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
As for intermediate non-informative action (*avijñapti*), it may be obtained either through performance (*kṛta*) or [by other means].
This refers to performing prostrations, praises, or even acts such as striking a *caitya* with a mind of intense passion or fierce afflictions.
Alternatively, it may be acquired through a formal undertaking (*samādāna*), such as making this resolve:
"I shall never eat first unless I have constructed a maṇḍala for the Buddha."
Such vows as these may be acquired through relinquishment; that is to say, by the construction of monasteries, dwellings, bedding, and gardens, or by making offerings to bhikṣus and others.
One relinquishes this non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) because both the motivating mind and the performed action have been severed and destroyed.

Thus, the unmanifest (avijñapti) and the five sense faculties previously mentioned, such as the eye, are objects cognized solely by the mental consciousness; up to this point, they are termed the first category of matter (rūpa-padārtha).
However, the characteristics of all phenomena are briefly of three kinds:
first, specific and general characteristics;
second, partial general characteristics.
3. The universal common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the individual and common characteristics: for example, because it undergoes transformation and decay, or because it offers resistance, it is called "form" (*rūpa*).
This explains the meaning of being susceptible to affliction and destruction, as the Dharma King has said:
"O bhikṣus, you should know that it is called the 'appropriation-aggregate of form' (rūpôpādāna-skandha) because of its susceptibility to transformation and decay.
What is able to transform and decay it?
It is, for example, the touch of the hand; thus it transforms and decays, and so forth, as explained at length."
Just as one is called a "horse" because of the ability to gallop, and is designated as a "cow" and so forth because of the ability to walk;
so too are the specific characteristics divided, such as the nature of impermanence, the nature of suffering, and so forth.
The universal common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) refers to such qualities as the nature of non-self (*anātmatva*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
By this same principle, one should understand that all phenomena possess these three characteristics.
Regarding the category of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), it refers to the three types of experience:
First, pleasure;
second, suffering;
third, neither-suffering-nor-pleasure—these are the meanings of the three types of experience that follow contact.
It arises from contact that is pleasant, unpleasant, or neither;
it is produced by the specific states of body and mind, characterized by joy, sorrow, or neutrality toward objects; and because it serves as the cause for craving, it is called "feeling" (*vedanā*).
As the Blessed One has said:
"Contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving.
Furthermore, these follow the distinctions of consciousness and are sixfold, namely: feeling born of eye-contact, up to and including feeling born of mind-contact.

That which arises together with the five consciousnesses is called bodily sensation (*kāyikī vedanā*); that which arises together with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is called mental sensation (*caitasikī vedanā*).

Based on the distinctions among the faculties (*indriya*), five types are established: namely, the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
The pleasant bodily sensations and the mental pleasant sensations of the third dhyāna are called the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
"Pleasant" has the meaning of being beneficial.
All unpleasant bodily sensations are called the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
Displeasure has the meaning of affliction and harm.
With the exception of the third dhyāna, all other mental feelings of pleasure are called the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
All mental feelings of displeasure are called the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
The sensation that is neither pleasant nor unpleasant, pertaining to both body and mind, is called the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
This is explained in detail in the section on the faculties (*indriya-varga*).
As for the meaning of the term "perception" (*saṃjñā*), it refers to the conceptual understanding that joins together signs (*nimitta*) with names (*nāman*) and meanings (*artha*).

It is the conceptualizing of blue, yellow, long, short, and so forth; of sounds such as those of conch shells and drums; of fragrances such as agarwood and musk; of tastes such as salty and bitter; of tactile objects such as hardness and softness; and of the characteristics, names, and meanings of phenomena such as male and female—synthesizing these through mental construction—and serving as the cause for vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought); therefore, it is called saṃjñā (perception).
These [perceptions] are of six types according to their respective consciousnesses, just like feeling (*vedanā*).
There are three distinctions based on small, great, and immeasurable [objects]: that which takes a limited object as its domain is called "small perception" (*parīttasaṃjñā*);

that which takes great dharmas such as the sublime (*brahmavihāra*) and so forth as its domain is called "great perception" (*mahāsaṃjñā*); [and that which takes an immeasurable object as its domain is called "immeasurable perception"].
The designations "boundless" (*apramāṇa*) follow from [the meditative attainments] such as the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
Alternatively, these three names are established in accordance with the three realms (*tridhātu*).
There are two kinds of formations (*saṃskāra*): namely, associated formations (*cittasaṃprayuktasaṃskāra*) and dissociated formations (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*).

Associated mental factors (*saṃprayukta-dharma*) refer to volition, contact, desire, attention, resolve, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, vitarka, vicāra, faith, diligence, shame, dread, heedfulness, pliancy, non-harming, equanimity, joy, aversion, lack of faith, laziness, heedlessness, the roots of goodness, the roots of unwholesomeness, the roots of the indeterminate, the fetters, bonds, latent tendencies, secondary afflictions, envelopments, outflows, floods, yokes, graspings, bodily ties, hindrances, as well as knowledge, patience, and so forth—all such mental factors are termed "associated" because they are equal to the mind in five respects: their basis, object, aspect, time, and substance.

That which is contrary to this is called "non-associated," namely: acquisition (*prāpti*), non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the homogeneous character of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*), birth (*jāti*), duration (*sthiti*), aging (*jarā*), impermanence (*anityatā*), and the groups of names (*nāma-kāya*), phrases (*pada-kāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*).
These conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that are associated and dissociated are collectively termed the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
Therefore, the Great Sage said:
"The accumulation of the aggregate of formations is like the trunk of a plantain tree."
Volition (*cetanā*) refers to that which causes the mind to engage in activity; it is precisely mental action (*manas-karman*), and its meaning is also that of setting the mind in motion.
Because it is distinguished as wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, it has three distinct types.

Contact (*sparśa*) arises from the conjunction of the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness; it causes the mind to touch the object and has the characteristic of being able to nourish the mental factors (*caitta*). It is divided into three types according to its conformity with pleasant feeling and so forth.
*Chanda* (desire) refers to the seeking after and the undertaking of an activity; it accords with *vīrya* (diligence), in the sense that one thinks, "I shall perform such an activity.

*Manasikāra* (attention) refers to that which causes the mind to be alert; its meaning is to lead the mind toward an object, and it also consists of the recollection of what was previously experienced and so forth. This has three types: those of the learner (*śaikṣa*), those of the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), and those who are neither learners nor non-learners (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).

The untainted attention within the body of one in training is called "in training" (śaikṣa); the untainted attention within the body of an arhat is called "beyond training" (aśaikṣa); and all tainted attention is called "neither in training nor beyond training" (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
Resolve (adhimokṣa) refers to the ability to affirm an object; that is, it means causing the mind to be free from timidity regarding its focal object.
Mindfulness (smṛti) refers to causing the mind to clearly remember an object; that is, not forgetting it.
"Past," "present," and "future" refer to the meaning of activity.
"Concentration" (samādhi) means causing the mind to focus one-pointedly on a single object; it is the sense of restraining the monkey-like mind so that it functions only upon a single object.
The *Vibhāṣā* masters explain it as follows: just as a snake moving within a tube does not bend, so too when the mind is in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it proceeds with rectitude.

"Wisdom" (*prajñā*) refers to the capacity for discernment regarding phenomena; that is, it takes as its object the investigation, as appropriate, of the eight types of phenomena—namely, those comprised by the causes, conditions, and fruits of association and accomplishment, including both specific and general characteristics.
Vitarka (investigation) is defined as having the characteristic of making the mind coarse with respect to its object; it is also termed conceptualization and discursive thought.
Bound by the wind of perception (*saṃjñā*), it functions as a coarse movement; this dharma is precisely the cause for the arising of the five consciousnesses.
Investigation (*vicāra*) has the characteristic of making the mind subtle with respect to its object; this dharma is the cause that enables the mental consciousness to proceed toward its object.

Faith (*śraddhā*) causes the mind to be clear and pure with respect to its object; it consists of the present acceptance and conviction regarding the Three Jewels, the causal relationship between actions and their results, and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and is therefore called faith.

This is the dharma that can dispel the turbidity and impurities of the mind; it is like placing a water-clearing jewel into a pond, causing all turbid and foul water to immediately become clear and pure.
In this way, when the jewel of faith is within the pond of the mind, all the turbidity and impurities of the mind are immediately dispelled.

To have faith that the Buddha has realized awakening, faith that the Dharma is well-expounded, faith that the Saṅgha possesses sublime conduct, and furthermore, faith in the nature of dependent origination which all non-Buddhists are deluded about—this is the activity of faith.

Vigor (vīrya) has the nature of being courageous and resolute regarding the arising and ceasing of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena; it is the sense of being able to exert the mind so that one who is submerged in the mire of saṃsāra may quickly emerge from it.

*Hrī* (moral shame) refers to the state of mental sovereignty that opposes the outflow of craving and so forth, which arises through the predominant influence of conforming to correct principles and pure dharmas; by the power of this, one dwells with reverence toward all virtues and those who possess virtue.

*Hrī* (moral shame) refers to taking the cultivation of meritorious qualities as primary; it is the reproaching of inferior phenomena that flow from delusion, and by its power, one perceives dread in transgressions.
*Apramāda* (heedfulness) refers to the cultivation of all wholesome dharmas; it is the opposition to and subversion of negligence, whereby one guards the nature of the mind.
The pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) of the mind is defined as its serviceability; it opposes and counteracts lethargy (*styāna*) and accords with wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*).

The non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) of the mind is defined as its firm and wholesome nature; by this power, one does not injure or afflict others, and is able to oppose those who would seek to cause harm to others.

The equanimity of the mind is called *upekṣā* (equanimity), because it turns away from what is unreasonable and inclines toward what is reasonable. By the power of this, the mind neither inclines toward nor turns away from the reasonable and the unreasonable, abiding in equality like the string of a balance scale.

"Joy" (prāmodya) refers to the state of admiring the category of cessation (nirodha-pakṣa). Having perceived its merits, it causes the mind to aspire to and accord with the cultivation of virtue; because the mind possesses this quality, one takes delight in nirvāṇa. That which is associated with this is called "joyful attention" (prāmodya-manasikāra).

Disgust refers to the state of being weary of the category of cyclic existence; having perceived its faults, it causes the mind to become detached and conforms to freedom from defilement. Because the mind possesses this quality, one loathes birth and death; the mental attention associated with this is called "the attention of disgust."
A mind that is not clear and pure is called lack of faith; it is the opposite of the characteristics of faith described previously.
A mind that lacks mental vigor is called laziness; it is the opposite of the previously described diligence.

Not cultivating wholesome dharmas constitutes heedlessness (*pramāda*), which contradicts the previously explained nature of non-heedlessness (*apramāda*); this is precisely the meaning of being unable to guard the mind.

As for the three factors—lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) and so forth—that were mentioned above, they are not established as *anuśaya*, *paryavasthāna*, or *upakleśa* because their faults are slight and they are easily eliminated.
There are three kinds of roots of goodness:
first, non-attachment, which is the dharma that opposes attachment;
second, non-hatred, which is the dharma that opposes hatred.
Third, non-delusion (*amoha*) is the factor that opposes delusion; its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the aforementioned wisdom (*prajñā*).

These three factors constitute the intrinsic nature of the wholesome and are also able to serve as roots from which other wholesome factors arise; therefore, they are called "wholesome roots" (*kuśalamūla*).

The meaning of "secure" (*kṣema*) is the meaning of "wholesome" (*kuśala*), because it leads to the sprouts of desirable existence and liberation; alternatively, the meaning of "wholesome" is that which has been practiced until skillfulness is achieved, for by means of this one can produce exquisite forms and images—just as a painter who creates exquisite forms and images is praised by the world as "skillful."
There are three types of unwholesome roots, namely the three—greed, hatred, and delusion—that were previously identified as the objects of counteraction.

"Greed" refers to the five categories of greed in the desire realm; "hatred" refers to the five categories of hatred; and "delusion" refers to the thirty-four instances of ignorance in the desire realm, excluding the ignorance associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

These three factors are unwholesome by their very nature (*svabhāva-akuśala*), and because they can also serve as roots that give rise to other unwholesome states, they are called "unwholesome roots" (*akuśalamūla*).

The meaning of being "unwholesome" is the sense of being "insecure" (*an-āśvāsa*), because they draw forth the sprouts of undesirable existences (*bhava*). Alternatively, the meaning of being "unwholesome" is the sense of being "unskillful" due to a lack of training and learning, because through this [lack of skill] one produces inferior forms and appearances; just as when a painter creates something poorly, the world calls it "unwholesome."
There are four kinds of neutral roots (*avyākṛta-mūla*), namely: craving (*tṛṣṇā*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).
Craving refers to the greed (*rāga*) of five categories each within the form and formless realms.

Views refer to the twelve types of views in each of the form and formless realms, as well as the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of extreme attachment (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) in the desire realm.
Pride refers to the five types of pride in each of the form and formless realms.
Ignorance refers to all ignorance in the form and formless realms, as well as the ignorance associated with the view of a self-identity and the view of extreme attachment in the desire realm.
These four neutral roots are so designated because those who practice meditative concentration (dhyāna) are held to be of three distinct types:
first, those for whom craving predominates; second, those for whom views predominate; and third, those for whom pride predominates. All three of these arise through the power of ignorance (avidyā).
The *Vibhāṣā* masters establish that there are only three neutral roots (*avyākṛta-mūla*), namely: neutral craving (*tṛṣṇā*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Doubt (*vicikitsā*) is not firm or stable, and the view of self-existence (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) is characterized by haughtiness; because they lack the nature of a root, they are not included. They are called "neutral" (*avyākṛta*) because they are not defined as either wholesome or unwholesome.
Furthermore, because they cannot be designated as having either pleasant or unpleasant results, they are called "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*).

Since they cannot induce a ripened result (*vipāka-phala*), they are of an indeterminate nature; yet, because they can also give rise to other indeterminate defiled states or various indeterminate phenomena, they are termed "indeterminate roots."

There are nine kinds of fetters, namely: the fetter of craving, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of pride, the fetter of ignorance, the fetter of views, the fetter of grasping, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of envy, and the fetter of avarice.
The fetter of craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*) refers to greed within the three realms; it has the characteristic of stained attachment, like melted glue or lacquer, and is therefore called "craving.
Since craving itself is a fetter, it is termed the "fetter of craving."

The fetter of malice (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) refers to the hatred belonging to the five categories; it consists in the desire to inflict harm and suffering upon sentient beings and others. Because its characteristic is non-beneficial, like the seeds of bitter plants, it is called "malice."
Hatred itself is a fetter; therefore, it is called the fetter of hatred (*pratigha-saṃyojana*).

As for the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*), it refers to the pride of the three realms. When one distinguishes oneself from others based on differences in qualities and types, the mental state of haughty exaltation is termed "pride," just as an arrogant person treats others with contempt.
This further comprises seven types:
first, pride; second, excessive pride; [and so forth].
3. Pride beyond pride;
4. the pride of "I am";
5. overweening pride;
Sixth, inferiority-conceit (*ūnamāna*);
seventh, false conceit (*mithyāmāna*).

That is to say, based on such matters as one's lineage, wealth, status, physical appearance, strength, observance of precepts, extensive learning, or artistic skill, if one regards oneself as superior to those who are inferior, or regards oneself as equal to those who are equal, the resulting elevation of the mind is termed conceit (*māna*).

If one considers oneself superior to those who are equal, or considers oneself equal to those who are superior, and by this causes the mind to become haughty, it is called *abhimāna* (overweening pride).
If one considers oneself superior to those who are actually superior, and by this causes the mind to become haughty, it is called *mānātimāna* (pride beyond pride).
If one clings to the five aggregates of clinging as "I" or "mine," and by means of this causes the mind to become uplifted, it is called *asmimāna* (the pride of "I am").

If one claims to have realized superior qualities, such as the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*), when they have not yet been realized, and by means of this causes the mind to become uplifted, it is called *abhimāna* (overweening pride).

If, amidst those who are largely superior in terms of lineage and other such qualities, one considers oneself slightly inferior, yet this causes the mind to become uplifted, it is called *ūnamāna* (inferiority conceit).
If one actually lacks virtue yet claims to possess virtue, and this causes the mind to become uplifted, it is called *mithyāmāna* (false conceit).
These seven types of pride are collectively termed the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*).

As for the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*), it refers to the lack of knowledge regarding the three realms; its characteristic is a failure to understand and comprehend. Because it obstructs and harms clarity, just as one who is blind and sightless is hindered from seeing, it is called "ignorance" (*avidyā*).
This negating expression functions according to the sense of an antidote, just as terms such as "non-friend" or "unreal" refer respectively to an enemy or to false speech.
Ignorance itself is a fetter; therefore, it is called the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*).

As for the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), it refers to the three views: namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), and false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*).

Within the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), there is no self (*ātman*) nor anything belonging to a self (*ātmīya*); yet, to grasp at them as having the characteristics of a real self and what belongs to a self—this defiled wisdom is called the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
"Body" (*kāya*) has the meaning of an accumulation; because it exists and is a body, it is called "the body that exists" (*satkāya*).
The five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) are what is referred to as the "view of a self-identity" (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) when one perceives them in this way.

To grasp at these same five aggregates of clinging—which are neither annihilated nor eternal—as having the two characteristics of annihilation and permanence, is the defiled wisdom called the "view of extremes" (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), because it clings to the two extremes.

If one dogmatically adheres to the view that there is no karma and no fruit of karma, no liberation and no path to attain liberation, thereby repudiating actual reality, this defiled wisdom is called wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
These three views are called the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).

As for the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*), it refers to the two types of grasping: namely, the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*) and the grasping of precepts and observances (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*).

This means that regarding the aforementioned three views and the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*), which are in reality not superior, one grasps them as being superior; this defiled wisdom is called the grasping of views.
"Grasping" (*parāmarśa*) has the meaning of seeking and stubborn adherence. "Precepts" (*śīla*) refers to distancing oneself from the evils of broken precepts.

"Vows" (*vrata*) refers to the observance of practices such as those of the crow, the cock, the deer, or the dog; going naked or plucking out one's hair; fasting or lying in ashes; or, based on false attachments, performing frequent ablutions in various rivers and ponds to generate merit and extinguish sin; or sustaining one's life by eating roots, fruits, grasses, vegetables, and medicinal herbs; or smearing oneself with ash and plucking out one's hair—these are all termed "vows."

These two are both not the path capable of purifying, yet they are falsely grasped as being the path capable of purifying; this defiled wisdom is called the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

Among the Brahmins, many who are learned cling to these dharmas as the path to purity, yet they are unable to attain ultimate purification. Such dualistic clinging is termed the fetter of clinging (*parāmarśasaṃyojana*).

The fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) refers to causing the mind to waver with hesitation regarding the Four Noble Truths. It is like seeing a figure made of bound grass at a crossroads and being unable to decide; likewise, one wavers regarding the mind [realizing] suffering, wondering whether it is so or not, and so forth, as explained in detail.
Doubt itself is a fetter; therefore, it is called the "fetter of doubt.

As for the "fetter of envy," it refers to the mind's inability to endure another's excellence. That is, when one encounters another’s receiving of respect, offerings, wealth, status, extensive learning, or other superior qualities, the mind gives rise to jealousy; this is the meaning of "inability to endure."
Envy itself is a fetter; therefore, it is called the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*).

As for the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*), it refers to the mind being characterized by avarice regarding one's own dharmas and wealth, thinking, "May what belongs to me not go to others."
Avarice itself is a fetter; therefore, it is called the "avarice-fetter.
The meaning of "fetter" (saṃyojana) is the meaning of "bondage. As the Blessed One said:
"It is not that form is fettered by the eye, nor that the eye is fettered by form; rather, the desire and greed therein are what are called 'fetters.'"
Just as a black ox does not bind a white ox, nor does a white ox bind a black ox— and so forth, as explained at length—
the fetters previously mentioned are also bonds, because the very meaning of "fetter" (*saṃyojana*) is the meaning of "bond" (*bandhana*).
However, the sūtras further speak of three fetters (*bandhana*):
first, the fetter of attachment (*rāga-bandhana*), which refers to all forms of greed, as described in the characteristics of the fetter of craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*).
Second, the fetter of aversion (*pratigha-bandhana*), which refers to all forms of anger, as described in the characteristics of the fetter of hostility (*pratigha-saṃyojana*).
Third, the bond of delusion (*moha-bandhana*), which refers to all forms of delusion as described in the definition of the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*).
There are seven types of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*): first, the latent disposition of sensual desire (*kāmarāga-anuśaya*); [and so forth].
2. the latent tendency of aversion;
3. the latent tendency of sensual desire;
4. the latent tendency of pride;
5. The latent tendency of ignorance;
6. the latent tendency of views;
7. the latent tendency of doubt.
These seven specific characteristics have already been explained among the fetters (*saṃyojana*).

However, one should distinguish these seven kinds of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) according to their realms (*dhātu*), modes of activity (*ākāra*), and categories (*nikāya*); that is to say, because it craves various sensual desires, it is called "sensual craving" (*kāmarāga*).
This greed itself is the latent tendency (*anuśaya*); therefore, it is called the latent tendency of sensual greed (*kāmarāgānuśaya*).

This consists of five types corresponding to the five categories of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), namely: those to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) up to those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
The latent tendency of aversion (*pratighānuśaya*) consists of five types, corresponding to the five categories of the desire realm alone.

The latent tendency of sensual greed (*rāgānuśaya*) consists of ten types, corresponding to the five categories each of the form and formless realms, because it operates with respect to internal objects.
In order to exclude the notion that the dhyānas and formless attainments are liberations, the craving for the two realms is termed "craving for existence" (bhavarāga).
As for the latent tendency of pride (mānānuśaya), it pervades all three realms across five categories each, totaling fifteen.
The latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) is likewise. The latent tendencies of views (*dṛṣṭi-anuśaya*) pertain to all three realms and consist of twelve for each, totaling thirty-six.

Specifically, in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), those abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) possess all five views; those abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) and cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) possess only two—false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*); and those abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*) possess only three—false view, grasping at views, and grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). These together constitute twelve. The same applies to the two higher realms, thus totaling thirty-six.

The latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*) comprises twelve types across the three realms, consisting of four categories for each—namely, those to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
Among these, the latent tendencies of sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and aversion (*pratigha*) differ only by category (*pakṣa*), but not by realm (*dhātu*) or aspect (*ākāra*).
The latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of attachment, doubt, pride, and ignorance possess distinctions of realm (*dhātu*) and category (*nikāya*), but lack distinctions of aspect (*ākāra*).
The latent tendency of views possesses distinctions of realm, aspect, and category.
Regarding the distinction of their modes of activity (*ākāra*): that which operates with the mode of "self and what belongs to self" is called the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

That which operates with the mode of annihilationism or eternalism is called the view of extreme adherence (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). That which operates with the mode of negation is called false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). That which operates with the mode of superiority is called the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). That which operates with the mode of purity is called the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
The meaning of "subtle" (*anu*) is the meaning of "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*), because it is difficult to perceive when it manifests.

Alternatively, the meaning of "binding along with" (*anuśayana*) is the meaning of "latent tendency," meaning that it evolves in accordance with the bondage of body and mind, just as a shadow moving through the air follows one moving through water.
Alternatively, the meaning of "proclivity" (*anuśaya*) is the sense of "following along," just as oil resides in sesame seeds or moisture resides in a lump of dough.

Alternatively, the meaning of "proclivity" is the sense of "increasing along with," meaning that [the proclivities] increase in accordance with their objects (*ālambana*) and mental associations (*samprayoga*) within the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*).
Regarding the term "increasing in accordance" (*anuśerate*), it means that they increase by way of their objects (*ālambana*) and their associated factors (*samprayoga*).
These seven types of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), through the distinctions of realms (*dhātu*), aspects (*ākāra*), and categories (*pakṣa*), constitute ninety-eight latent dispositions.

This refers to the ten underlying tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*): namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the esteeming of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), greed (*rāga*), hatred (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).

There are seven underlying tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin; these are the same as the ten previously mentioned, excluding the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi), and the clinging to rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
There are likewise seven underlying tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of cessation.
There are eight underlying tendencies abandoned through the path of seeing, namely the aforementioned seven plus the view of adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
There are four underlying tendencies abandoned through the path of cultivation, namely greed, hatred, pride, and ignorance.
Thus, there are thirty-six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

There are thirty-one underlying tendencies in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), which means that from the thirty-six of the desire realm, the five categories of aversion (*dveṣa*) are excluded. It is the same for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); therefore, there are ninety-eight underlying tendencies in total.
Among these, eighty-eight are abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) and ten are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

Thirty-three are universal (*sarvatraga*), namely: within each realm, the views and doubts abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin, along with their associated and unshared ignorance (*avidyā*); all others are non-universal.

Eighteen are those with uncontaminated objects (*anāsravālambana*); that is to say, within each realm, the false views, doubts, and their associated or independent ignorance (*avidyā*) that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path.
These eighteen types of conditions take cessation and the path as their objects; therefore, they are called "untainted objects" (*anāsrava-ālambana*).
All others have tainted objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*). Among these, those with tainted objects increase in accordance [with the defilements] by virtue of both their objects and their association.
Regarding those with uncontaminated objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*), they increase only within their own group by way of association (*saṃprayoga*).

Nine have the unconditioned as their object (*asaṃskṛta-ālambana*): namely, among the realms, the false view, doubt, and the associated and non-associated ignorance (*avidyā*) that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*).
Because it takes the Truth of Cessation as its object, it is called "conditioned by the unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta-pratyaya*); all others are conditioned by the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-pratyaya*).

Regarding the sequential arising of the ten types of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*): first, due to ignorance, one lacks clear understanding of the Truths; that is, regarding suffering, one has no desire for it, and so on, up to having no desire for the Path.

Due to this lack of understanding, doubt subsequently arises; that is, upon hearing the two categories of the false and the correct, one harbors hesitation as to whether [phenomena] are suffering or not suffering, and so on, up to whether they are the path or not the path.

From this doubt, wrong view is induced; that is to say, through improper hearing and reflection, an evil friend gives rise to a false certainty, [thinking]: "There is no giving, there is no offering, there is no sacrifice," and so forth, as explained at length.

From this false view, the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arises; that is, by denying the principle of suffering within the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*), one then clings to the notion of a self or what belongs to a self.
From the view of a self-entity, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) arises; that is, because one clings to the extremes of annihilationism or eternalism regarding the self.

From the view of extreme attachment (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) arises, because this extreme attachment is regarded as being capable of purification.
From the clinging to precepts and observances, the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) arises, because that which is considered capable of purification is regarded as being supreme.
From this grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), greed (*rāga*) is subsequently induced, because of the deep affection felt for one's own views.
Following this greed, pride (*māna*) is subsequently induced, because once one is deeply attached to one's own views, one relies upon them to give rise to loftiness and to treat others with contempt.

Following this pride, anger is subsequently induced; that is to say, because one who relies on their own view cannot endure the views of others and will inevitably feel resentment and aversion toward them, or because they give rise to resentment and aversion during the process of adopting or rejecting their own views.
The sequence of the ten types of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) is as follows.
Afflictions arise due to three causes and conditions:
first, because the latent dispositions have not been abandoned;
Second, due to improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*);
third, due to the presence of the object (*viṣaya*).
Through these three powers—of cause, application, and object—the afflictions manifest; this refers to the case where all factors are present.

There are also those that arise solely through the power of their objects, causing turbulence and pervasive affliction throughout the continuity of body and mind; therefore, they are called *kleśas* (afflictions).
These are precisely the *anuśayas* (latent tendencies).
As for the *upakleśas* (secondary afflictions), all *kleśas* are also termed *upakleśas*.

Furthermore, there are secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), namely all other defiled mental factors (*citta-saṃprayukta-dharma*) subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), because they are included within the same aggregate as the primary afflictions. What, then, are these?
These refer to deception, arrogance, malice, vexation, resentment, guile, and so forth, of which there are immeasurable varieties as taught in the Noble Teachings.
Deception (*māyā*) means deluding others.

Arrogance (*mada*) means that, having become attached to one's own physical beauty, strength, lineage, pure precepts, extensive learning, or skillful eloquence, the mind becomes haughty and dissolute, characterized by a lack of regard for anything else.
*Vihiṃsā* (harmfulness) refers to the ability to inflict oppression upon others, by means of which one engages in acts such as beating and reviling.
*Pradāsa* (malice) refers to the stubborn adherence to blameworthy matters, by means of which one does not accept reasoned admonition.
Resentment (*upanāha*) refers to the repeated contemplation of an object of anger, maintaining a grudge without relinquishing it.
Deceit (*śāṭhya*) refers to mental crookedness.
These six types arise from the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The coarse characteristics of defilement are called the stains of affliction (*kleśamala*).
Among these six kinds of stains of affliction, the two types—deceit (*māyā*) and arrogance (*mada*)—are outflows of greed (*lobha*), as they belong to the category of greed.
The two types, *pradāśa* (malice) and *upanāha* (enmity), are outflows (*niṣyanda*) of hatred (*dveṣa*), because they belong to the category of hatred.

*Pradāśa* (agitation) is an outflow of the view of grasping at inferior views as superior (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), because one who clings to their own views as supreme causes distress to both themselves and others.
The stain of flattery (*śāṭhya*) is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the various views, for views increase through flattery and crookedness.

As it is said: "Flattery refers to the various evil views. This stain, along with its associated entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) and other factors subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), is defiled.
All mental factors that arise from the afflictions are termed secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

There are ten types of entanglements (*paryavasthāna*): namely, lethargy (*styāna*), torpor (*middha*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), anger (*krodha*), and concealment (*mrakṣa*).

The state of the continuity of body and mind being unserviceable is called *styāna* (sloth); it has the sense of being dull and heavy. The inability to sustain the continuity of body and mind, causing the mind to become dim and withdrawn, is called *middha* (torpor).
These receive the name "envelopers" (*paryavasthāna*) solely by virtue of being defiled.
Excitement (*auddhatya*) refers to that which causes the mind to lack tranquility.
The essence of what is poorly done is termed "regret" (*kaukṛtya*).

There is a distinct mental factor that arises with remorse as its object; it is designated by the name "remorse" (*kaukṛtya*), which carries the meaning of "regret. This is a case of metaphorically applying the name of the cause to the nature of the effect, just as one speaks of "emptiness" when referring to what is empty, or "impurity" when referring to what is impure.
The world also speaks of a basis by way of its location, as when one says, "all [people] from the villages and towns have come," and so forth.
This establishment of the name "enwrapment" (paryavasthāna) likewise depends solely upon defilement.
The two characteristics of envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) have already been explained among the fetters (*saṃyojana*).

That which causes the mind to lack reverence toward various merits and those who possess merit is called lack of shame (*āhrīkya*); it is the state of being diametrically opposed to respect (*gaurava*).
Not perceiving fear toward any misdeeds is called *anapatrāpya* (lack of moral dread); it leads to rebirth in the evil realms, is censured by the virtuous, and is termed a transgression.
Apart from hatred (*dveṣa*) and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*), that which causes the mind to flare up with indignation toward sentient and insentient objects is called *krodha* (anger).
Concealing one's own faults is called *mrakṣa* (concealment).
These ten are called *paryavasthāna* (envelopments) because they envelop the continuity of body and mind.
Among these, lethargy (*styāna*), sleep (*middha*), and lack of shame (*anapatrāpya*) are the outflows (*niṣyanda*) of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Regret is the outflow of doubt.
Lack of shame, stinginess, and restlessness are the outflows of greed.
Envy and anger are the outflows of hatred.
Concealment (*mrakṣa*) is an outflow (*niṣyanda*) of greed (*lobha*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and so forth.

Since the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) are subtle in their modes of activity (*ākāra*), it is already difficult to discern each one in its continuous succession, let alone when they exist simultaneously in a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).

Those of subtle and profound wisdom, relying on what the Buddha has taught, observe the distinctions among results and thereby know their differing natures; they then proclaim this without error to those who are training.

However, those of inferior intelligence—who have not personally served teachers who provide unerring explanations of the Buddha’s words—are confused and mistaken regarding mental factors (*caitta*), and thus either deny them altogether or claim that there are only three.
There are three kinds of outflows (*āsrava*): namely, the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).
The afflictions (*kleśa*) and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) of the desire realm, excluding ignorance, are called the outflow of desire.
There are forty-one entities, namely the thirty-one latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) together with the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).
The afflictions and envelopments of the form and formless realms, excluding ignorance (*avidyā*), are termed "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).

There are fifty-four entities: namely, the twenty-six latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of each of the two upper realms, together with lethargy (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*). Because these are equally indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), because they function internally, and because they depend on the stages of meditative concentration (*samādhi-bhūmi*), the two realms are combined and established under the single designation of "contaminated" (*sāsrava*).

Ignorance pertaining to the three realms is called the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*); it consists of fifteen entities. Because ignorance is the root of all existence (*bhava*), it is established separately as an outflow and so forth.
It is called an "outflow" (*āsrava*) because it causes sentient beings to linger and remain long within the three realms, thereby obstructing their progress toward liberation.
Alternatively, they are called "outflows" (*āsrava*) because they cause one to transmigrate from the Peak of Existence down to the Avīci Hell;
or, they are called "outflows" because that continuity leaks inexhaustibly through the six wounds of the sense gates.
There are four floods (*ogha*), namely: the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*), the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*), the flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*), and the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*).
Within the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsava*), excluding views, is termed the flood of desire; it consists of twenty-nine entities.
Within the outflows (*āsrava*), excluding the views, they are called the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*), consisting of thirty entities.
The various views of the three realms are called the flood of views (*dṛṣṭy-ogha*), consisting of thirty-six entities.
The non-specific ignorance associated with the three realms is called the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*), which consists of fifteen entities.
It is termed a "flood" because it sweeps away and carries off all the superior qualities of sentient beings, just as a torrential flood of water does.
There are four kinds of yokes (*yoga*), as explained in the section on the floods (*ogha*).
They are called "yokes" because they bind sentient beings together, causing them to undergo suffering within the various destinies (*gati*), births (*upapatti*), and stages (*bhūmi*).
This refers to the meaning of combining [factors] so that one experiences various kinds of light and heavy suffering.
