Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by imperial decree:

There are four kinds of grasping (*upādāna*), namely: grasping at sensual desire (*kāma-upādāna*), grasping at views (*dṛṣṭi-upādāna*), grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-upādāna*), and grasping at the discourse on self (*ātman-vāda-upādāna*).

The flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*), when combined with ignorance (*avidyā*), is called the grasping of desire (*kāma-upādāna*); it consists of thirty-four entities, namely: five each of greed, hatred, pride, and ignorance; four instances of doubt; and ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).

When the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*) is combined with ignorance (*avidyā*), it is termed the clinging to the doctrine of self (*ātma-vāda-upādāna*); this consists of forty entities, namely ten each of greed (*rāga*), conceit (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*), along with eight instances of doubt (*vicikitsā*), as well as lethargy (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*).

Among the various views, excluding the attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), the remainder are called the attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*); these consist of thirty entities.
The attachment to precepts and observances consists of six entities, as it alone stands as an adversary to the Noble Path and deceives both the lay and monastic communities alike.

Among the five views, this one is established separately as "clinging" (*parāmarśa*), because householders are deluded by it and reckon such things as self-starvation, inhaling air, and leaping from mountain cliffs to be the path to heaven.
The monastic community is thus deluded by this, for they reckon that abandoning desirable objects and undertaking the ascetic virtues (*dhūtaguṇa*) constitutes the path to purification.

The meaning of "fuel" (*indhana*) is the meaning of "clinging" (*upādāna*); it causes the fire of karma to blaze forth and continue to grow. Just as fire blazes up because there is fuel, so too do the karmas of sentient beings grow because of the presence of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Furthermore, the meaning of "intense" (*tīkṣṇa*) is the meaning of "grasping" (*upādāna*), or the meaning of "enveloping" is the meaning of "grasping.
Just as a silkworm dies by enveloping itself within its cocoon, so too are sentient beings enveloped by the four graspings; they wander through birth and death, losing their life of wisdom.

There are four kinds of bodily fetters (*kāyagrantha*): namely, the bodily fetter of sensual desire (*abhidhyā*), the bodily fetter of ill-will (*vyāpāda*), the bodily fetter of attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and the bodily fetter of dogmatic adherence to the view that "this alone is the truth" (*tattvābhiniveśa*).

The five categories of craving belonging to the desire realm are called the first bodily fetter; the five categories of ill-will are called the second bodily fetter; the six types of attachment to precepts and observances are called the third bodily fetter; and the twelve types of views are called the fourth bodily fetter.

Because they are various fetters that bind sentient beings by means of their own entanglements, they are called "bodily bonds" (*kāyagrantha*); this signifies the meaning of a snare that ensnares the bodies of sentient beings.

There are five kinds of hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*): namely, the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill-will, the hindrance of torpor and drowsiness, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt.

The five classes of greed in the desire realm are called the first hindrance; the five classes of hatred are called the second hindrance; torpor and unwholesome sleep in the desire realm are called the third hindrance; restlessness and unwholesome remorse in the desire realm are called the fourth hindrance; and the four classes of doubt in the desire realm are called the fifth hindrance.
Because they obscure the Noble Path, as well as the detachment from desire and the roots of goodness associated with the preparatory practice for both, they are called "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*).
Regarding what was previously stated concerning the various realms, destinies, births, and stages, it should be explained that suffering is experienced therein.
What are the realms (*dhātu*), destinies (*gati*), births (*upapatti*), and stages (*bhūmi*)?
There are three realms: namely, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The desire realm consists of twenty locations, namely the eight great hells:
1. Saṃjīva (Reviving);
2. Kālasūtra (Black Rope);
3. Saṃghāta (Crushing).
Fourth, Raurava;
fifth, Mahāraurava;
sixth, Tapana;
Seventh, the Extremely Hot Hell;
eighth, the Uninterrupted Hell; together with the animal realm and the hungry ghost realm, these constitute ten.
There are four continents of humans:
1. Jambudvīpa; 2. Videhadvīpa; 3. Godānīyadvīpa;
Fourth, the continent of Kuru.
There are six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*):
first, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*).
2. The Heaven of the Thirty-three;
3. The Yāma Heaven; 4. The Tuṣita Heaven;
Fifth, the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations;
sixth, the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations.
Together, there are twenty locations.
The realm of form consists of sixteen abodes; that is to say, the first dhyāna has two abodes:
first, the Heaven of Brahma’s Retinue (Brahmapāriṣadya);
second, the Heaven of Brahma’s Ministers (Brahmapurohita).
The second dhyāna has three heavens:
first, the Heaven of Limited Light;
second, the Heaven of Infinite Light; [and third, the Heaven of Utmost Purity].
Third, the Ābhāsvara Heaven. Within the third dhyāna there are three heavens:
first, the Parīttaśubha Heaven; [second, the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven; and third, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven].
2. the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (Apramāṇaśubha);
3. the Heaven of Universal Purity (Śubhakṛtsna).
The fourth dhyāna consists of eight heavens:
1. The Heaven of No Clouds (Anabhraka);
2. The Heaven of Merit-Born (Puṇyaprasava);
3. The Heaven of Vast Results (Bṛhatphala).
4. The Heaven of No Affliction;
5. The Heaven of No Heat;
6. The Heaven of Excellent Manifestation;
Seventh, the Sudarśana Heaven;
eighth, the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
Together, these constitute sixteen locations.
The Great Brahmā realm is without perception and has no distinct location; therefore, it is not included among the eighteen.
Although the formless realm lacks locations such as upper or lower, there are four distinct types of birthplaces:
first, the Sphere of Infinite Space; [and so forth].
2. the sphere of infinite consciousness;
3. the sphere of nothingness;
4. the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
There are five types of destinies:
first, hell-beings (nāraka);
second, animals (tiryagyoni).
3. the realm of hungry ghosts; 4.
devas; 5. humans.
There are four modes of birth, namely: egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born.

There are eleven stages, namely: the desire realm, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna, the four dhyānas, and the four formless attainments; these constitute the eleven stages.

The desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*); the remaining nine stages (*bhūmi*) are both contaminated and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Within the realms, destinies, and modes of birth, they are exclusively contaminated.

Wisdom is of ten kinds, namely: dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, knowledge of others' minds, knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin, knowledge of cessation, knowledge of the path, knowledge of exhaustion, and knowledge of non-arising.

The untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) present within the preparatory, uninterrupted, liberation, and special progress paths regarding the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) and their causes in the desire realm, as well as that which exists within the stage of the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna-bhūmi), is called the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna).
Having constantly harbored self-clinging since beginningless time, one now first perceives the Dharma; therefore, it is called "Dharma-knowledge" (dharmajñāna).

The untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) present within the paths of preparation, uninterrupted, liberation, and advancement regarding the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the form and formless realms, as well as their causes and their cessation, along with all such knowledge within the stage of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), is called "subsequent knowledge" (anvayajñāna).
It is called "subsequent knowledge" (*anvaya-jñāna*) because it arises following the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*).

All contaminated wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*) is termed "conventional knowledge" (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*); this knowledge mostly operates upon conventional objects such as jars and garments, and is therefore called conventional knowledge.
This is of two kinds:
first, defiled; second, non-defiled.
Defiled [factors] are further of two kinds:
first, those of the nature of views;
second, those not of the nature of views.

There are five types of views: namely, the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the esteeming of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Those that are not views are the wisdom associated with doubt, greed, hatred, pride, ignorance, anger, and harmfulness.
Non-defiled [phenomena] are also of two kinds:
first, wholesome;
second, non-obscured neutral.
That which is non-obscured and indeterminate is not "view" because it does not involve inferential deliberation;
it is wisdom (*prajñā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*). As for that which is wholesome, if it is associated with the five consciousnesses, it is also not "view," but is wisdom and knowledge.
If it is associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it is mundane right view (*laukika-samyagdṛṣṭi*), which is both discernment (*prajñā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*).

The knowledge produced by meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that is able to cognize another’s present similar mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*)—whether bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), or a portion of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*)—is called the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
This is of two kinds:
first, with outflows (sāsrava);
second, without outflows (anāsrava).
Regarding "with outflows" (sāsrava): it refers to that which can cognize the minds and mental factors associated with the desire and form realms belonging to others.
Regarding "without outflows" (anāsrava), there are two types: first, the category of dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna-pakṣa); [second, the category of subsequent knowledge].
2. The Category of Subsequent Knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna-pakṣa*).
Regarding the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna-pakṣa*): it is the knowledge of the mental states and mental factors belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge.
Regarding the category of subsequent knowledge: it is the knowledge of the mental states and mental factors belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge.

This wisdom does not know matter, the unconditioned, or formations dissociated from mind; furthermore, it cannot know any faculties, stages, or persons belonging to the formless realm, nor any superior minds or mental factors of the past or future.

When untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) arises regarding the fruit-portion of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), operating with the aspects (*ākāra*) of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, it is called the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*).

When untainted wisdom arises regarding the cause-portion of the five aggregates of clinging, operating with the aspects of cause, origin, production, and condition, it is called the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*).

Regarding that cessation, there is untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that functions with the aspects (*ākāra*) of cessation, tranquility, excellence, and renunciation; this is called the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*).

Regarding the path that serves as the antidote for that [suffering] and leads to the attainment of nirvāṇa, there is untainted knowledge that functions with the aspects of path, correctness, achievement, and departure; this is called the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
There is untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that reflects as follows:

"Suffering has been known by me; its origin has been abandoned by me; its cessation has been realized by me; the path has been cultivated by me. This turning toward the aspect of exhaustion is called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*).
There is untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that reflects as follows:

"Suffering has already been known by me; it need not be known again," and so on, up to "The Path has already been cultivated by me; it need not be cultivated again. When it functions with the aspect of non-arising (*anutpāda-ākāra*), it is called the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
These latter two knowledges are not of the nature of vision (*darśana*) because they do not involve inferential deliberation (*anumāna*).
The knowledge of others' minds is exclusively of the nature of vision; the remaining six knowledges are both of the nature of vision and not of the nature of vision.
Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*); knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) pertains to both the contaminated and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*);

and the remaining eight knowledges are exclusively uncontaminated. Knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) takes only the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its object; knowledge of others' minds, suffering (*duḥkha*), origin (*samudaya*), and the path (*mārga*) take only the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) as their objects; and the remaining five knowledges pertain to both the conditioned and the unconditioned.

The knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origination have only contaminated objects as their conditions; the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path have only uncontaminated objects as their conditions; the remaining six knowledges pertain to both contaminated and uncontaminated objects as their conditions.
The dharma-knowledge exists in six stages, namely: the four dhyānas, the threshold concentration (anāgamya), and the intermediate concentration (dhyānāntara).
Subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) exists in nine stages, namely the preceding six stages and the lower three formless stages (*ārūpya*).
Knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) exists in four stages, namely the four dhyānas.

Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) exists in all stages. As for the remaining six knowledges, those belonging to the category of Dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) exist in six stages, while those belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge exist in nine stages.

There are eight types of patience (*kṣānti*), namely: the patiences of the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as the patiences of the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering, origin, cessation, and the path. These eight are the superior wisdoms capable of inducing definitive knowledge.
Because they involve the patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) of the principles of the Four Noble Truths, such as suffering, they are called "acceptances.

Among all forms of acceptance, these eight are exclusively the patience of observing phenomena (*dharmanidhyānakṣānti*); they are of the nature of vision (*darśana*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), but not of the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*).
The meaning of "ascertainment" (*niścaya*) is the meaning of "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
These eight [moments] involve a conceptualizing intention (*abhiprāya*) that has not yet ceased; because they have not yet reached definitive certainty (*pariccheda*), they are not called knowledge.

The receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) simultaneously destroys the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm; the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) arises simultaneously with the acquisition of that abandonment.

Patience (*kṣānti*) serves as the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), and knowledge (*jñāna*) serves as the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*); they act as antidotes to the ten types of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
It is like two people: one drives out a thief from within a house, while the other closes the door to prevent him from re-entering.

The receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) simultaneously eliminates the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the eighteen latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the form and formless realms; the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) arises simultaneously with the acquisition of their abandonment. The remainder is as previously explained.
These four minds are able to effect the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Truth of Suffering within the three realms;
it should be understood that there are likewise four minds each for the Truths of Origin, Cessation, and the Path.

These sixteen minds are able to effect the clear realization of the Four Truths within the three realms, severing the eighty-eight fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through vision, and thereby attaining the fruit of Stream-entry (*srotāpanna*).
The remaining ten types of latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation consist of four from the desire realm and three each from the form and formless realms, totaling ten.

The four types of the desire realm are like a bundle of reeds; they are divided collectively into nine grades, ranging from the highest-of-the-high (*adhimātra-adhimātra*) down to the lowest-of-the-low (*mṛdu-mṛdu*).

The path of counteraction, consisting of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), likewise has nine grades; that is, the lowest-of-the-low grade of the path can counteract the highest-of-the-high grade of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), up to the highest-of-the-high grade of the path which can counteract the lowest-of-the-low grade of latent tendencies.
When the six grades [of afflictions] are exhausted, one attains the fruit of Once-returner; when the nine grades are exhausted, one attains the fruit of Non-returner.

Just as in the desire realm there are four [categories] which are collectively divided into nine, and there are likewise nine grades of uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) and paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) that serve as their respective antidotes;

so it should be understood that the same applies to each of the four stages within the form and formless realms, wherein for each stage there are nine grades of both the remediable afflictions and their respective antidotes.

By gradually severing the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of those eight stages, up until the time when even the lowest-of-the-low grade of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is exhausted, one attains the fruit of Arhatship.
All paths existing between the four fruits, as well as the preceding path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), are termed the "four candidates" (*pratipannaka*).
Whichever fruit one is currently approaching is called the "candidate" (pratipannaka) for that fruit.
Thus, there are eight types of persons (pudgala): namely, those practicing the four paths and those abiding in the four fruits.
Thus, these paths and fruits are divided into six types based on their spiritual lineage (*gotra*): namely, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of dull or sharp faculties.
If they enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), during the fifteen moments of mind, they are designated as "followers by faith" (*śraddhānusārin*) or "followers by dharma" (*dharmānusārin*).

These two types, upon reaching the stage of the path of cultivation—specifically from the sixteenth moment of mind up to the diamond-like concentration—are called those resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).

These two types, when they reach the stage of no-more-learning—from the initial knowledge of exhaustion up to the final moment of mind—are called "liberation by occasion" (*samayavimukta*) and "unconditional liberation" (*asamayavimukta*).

"Et cetera" refers to the fact that there are immeasurable varieties of mental factors (*caitta*). Because they exist in dependence upon the mind, they are called "mental concomitants" (*caitasika-dharma*), just as [the term] "mine" (*mama*) [depends on "I"].
Such mental factors are termed "associated formations" (*samprayukta-saṃskāra*).
The non-associated formations are the opposite of these, namely acquisition (*prāpti*) and so forth.
Acquisition refers to the cause for designating a phenomenon as existing.
There are three kinds of phenomena:
First, pure; second, impure;
third, indeterminate.
"Pure" refers to faith and so forth; "impure" refers to greed and so forth; "indeterminate" refers to the mind of transformation and so forth.
To be endowed with these factors is called being "one who possesses dharmas.
To speak of the causes for this concentration is termed "attainment," "acquisition," or "accomplishment."

If it were the case that [the antidote] does not exist, then when afflictions such as greed manifest, those in training (śaikṣa) would no longer be noble ones (ārya), since they would lack uncontaminated (anāsrava) minds at that time.
Furthermore, if an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) were to give rise to a wholesome or neutral mind, they would at that moment have to be designated as one who has already abandoned defilement.

Furthermore, since noble ones and ordinary worldlings alike lack the attainment of nirvāṇa and are thus mutually similar, they should both be called ordinary worldlings, or else both be called noble ones.
As the Dharma King has said:

"One is called a noble one (ārya) because of having attained the accomplishment of the ten dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), having forever severed the five members," and so forth, as extensively explained.
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:

"O bhikṣus, you should know that if there are those who accomplish wholesome or unwholesome dharmas, I see that within the mental continuum of such sentient beings, the acquisition (prāpti) of the wholesome and unwholesome increases boundlessly."
He spoke thus:

"O bhikṣus, you should not compare the superiority or inferiority of sentient beings, nor should you falsely estimate the depth or shallowness of the qualities of a person (pudgala)," and so forth, as explained at length.
Therefore, we know that there must certainly be a real acquisition (*prāpti*) external to the dharmas themselves.
This is of two kinds:
first, that which was previously unobtained or already lost and is now acquired; second, that which, having been acquired, is not lost and is thus possessed (*samanvāgata*).
It should be understood that non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is the opposite of this.
With respect to which phenomena are there acquisition and non-acquisition?
Acquisition and non-acquisition exist with respect to one's own continuum (*saṃtati*) and the two types of cessation (*nirodha*).
It is not another continuum, because there is no such thing as a phenomenon that accomplishes another body.
It is not a non-continuum, because there is no such thing as a phenomenon that accomplishes a non-sentient entity.
Nor is it space, because there is no one who accomplishes space.
If that acquisition (*prāpti*) does not exist, non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) likewise does not exist.
There are three kinds of acquisition:
first, acquisition that follows like a shadow follows a form; second, acquisition that leads like a bull-king leads the way; and third, acquisition that follows behind like a calf follows its mother.

The first acquisition (*prāpti*) is for the most part like that of non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) dharmas; the second is for the most part like the acquisition of wholesome (*kuśala*) dharmas of the desire realm at the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisandhi*) when one dies in a higher realm and is born into the desire realm; the third is for the most part like the wisdoms consisting of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī prajñā*), excluding those acquisitions that are innate (*upapattilābhika*).

In this regard, a brief *vibhāṣā* should be made: namely, for wholesome and unwholesome matter (*rūpa*) bound to the desire realm, there is no acquisition obtained prior to birth; there is only simultaneous acquisition and subsequent acquisition. This excludes the supernormal powers of the eye and ear, as well as the mind capable of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*), and further excludes a small portion of those that are either modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*) or crafts (*śailpasthānika*) when they have been extensively practiced. All other remaining non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena, as well as obscured neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena, [are likewise subject to these acquisitions].
Manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*) possesses only simultaneous acquisition (*sahaja-prāpti*); because its power is weak, it lacks prior or subsequent acquisition.
As for all other dharmas, each may possess prior, subsequent, or simultaneous acquisition.

The acquisition (*prāpti*) of wholesome phenomena is exclusively wholesome; the acquisition of unwholesome phenomena is exclusively unwholesome; and the acquisition of indeterminate phenomena is exclusively indeterminate.

The acquisition of phenomena belonging to the desire realm is exclusively of the desire realm; the acquisition of phenomena belonging to the form realm is exclusively of the form realm; and the acquisition of phenomena belonging to the formless realm is exclusively of the formless realm.
The acquisition of untainted phenomena (anāsrava-dharma) pertains to both the three realms and untainted phenomena themselves.
Untainted phenomena refer to the Truth of the Path and the three unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta), for both are dissociated from the realms.

The acquisition (*prāpti*) of the Truth of the Path is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*); the acquisition of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) pertains to all three realms; and the acquisition of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) pertains to the realms of form and formlessness.
That which arises through the power of the Path falls within those respective realms, because that which arises through the power of the untainted Path is itself untainted.
The acquisition (*prāpti*) of untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) is generally said to be of four kinds:

the acquisition of phenomena belonging to those in training (*śaikṣa*) is exclusively of the training type; the acquisition of phenomena belonging to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is exclusively of the beyond-training type; and the acquisition of phenomena that are neither in training nor beyond training is of three kinds.

Regarding phenomena that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner: these refer to all contaminated phenomena, as well as the acquisition (*prāpti*) of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), which are exclusively neither-learner-nor-non-learner.

The acquisition of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is of the nature of training (*śaikṣa*): that which arises through the power of the path of training is exclusively of the nature of training, while that which arises through the power of the path of no-more-training (*aśaikṣa*) is exclusively of the nature of no-more-training.
That which arises through the power of the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*) is exclusively neither of the nature of training nor of the nature of no-more-training.

The acquisition (*prāpti*) of factors abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) is exclusively abandoned by seeing; the acquisition of factors abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) is exclusively abandoned by cultivation.
The acquisition of factors not to be abandoned (*aheya*) is of three kinds: namely, those abandoned by cultivation and those not to be abandoned.
Dharmas that are not to be abandoned (*aheya*) refer to the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

The acquisition (*prāpti*) of the Truth of the Path is exclusively not to be abandoned; the acquisition of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is exclusively to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because it is non-defiled and yet possesses outflows (*sāsrava*); therefore, this applies to the acquisition of analytical cessation.

Those arising through the power of the worldly path (*laukikamārga*) are to be abandoned only by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*); those arising through the power of the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*) are only non-abandonable (*aheya*).

All non-possessions (*aprāpti*) are comprised exclusively within the category of unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) nature; they do not possess the distinctions of meaning found in the aforementioned "possession" (*prāpti*).

However, each and every phenomenon of the past and future possesses non-possession (*aprāpti*) belonging to all three time periods; whereas a present phenomenon lacks non-possession of the present, because the nature of possession (*prāpti*) and non-possession are mutually exclusive.
There is no present dharma that can be accomplished, because it is not yet accomplished.
However, there is non-possession (*aprāpti*) of past and future dharmas.
For each dharma belonging to the desire, form, and formless realms, as well as for untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas, there is non-possession belonging to each of the three realms.
There is no non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) that is untainted (*anāsrava*), because within non-acquisition there exists the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
As it is said:
"What is the nature of an ordinary person?"
This refers to not obtaining the noble dharmas.
"Not obtaining" is merely another name for "non-possession" (aprāpti).
Furthermore, all forms of non-possession are exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta) in nature; therefore, they are not untainted (anāsrava).

Having already become free from the defilements of the third dhyāna but not yet free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna, there occurs the cessation of the mind and mental factors belonging to the level of the fourth dhyāna. There exists a dissociated dharma called the "attainment of non-perception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*); although it brings about the cessation of all mind and mental factors, this attainment is entered specifically for the purpose of eliminating perception, and is therefore named "non-perception."

Like the knowledge of others' minds, this attainment of non-perception is included within the wholesome fourth dhyāna; it arises only within the mental continuum of those who are not noble ones, because they enter this meditative state with the thought of seeking liberation.

The Noble One regards this state as being like an evil realm and feels a profound sense of weary detachment toward it; this is exclusively a state conducive to fixed experience, specifically experience to be felt in the next life.

This cessation of meditative attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is acquired through preparatory application rather than through the abandonment of defilements. It refers to the cessation of the mind and mental factors of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) by one who has already abandoned the defilements of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). Because there exists a dissociated factor (*viprayukta-dharma*) capable of causing the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) to continue in equilibrium, it is termed "meditative cessation."

This is comprised of the preparatory wholesome states (*prayoga-kuśala*) of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) ground; it is either to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*), to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*), or to be experienced indeterminately (*aniyatavedanīya*).
Having arisen in this meditative attainment, one attains parinirvāṇa before the maturation (*vipāka*) has been obtained; therefore, it is indeterminate.
This meditative absorption can induce the maturation of the four aggregates within the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), for that realm lacks form.
Noble ones (*ārya*) are able to produce it, whereas ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) cannot, because this absorption is produced through the power of the Noble Path.

The Noble Ones seek to give rise to this meditative absorption in order to attain the blissful dwelling in the present life; whereas ordinary beings fear its cessation, and because they lack the power of the Noble Path, they are unable to give rise to it.

For noble ones, this [attainment] is acquired through application (*prayoga*) and not through detachment (*vairāgya*); only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, acquires this attainment of cessation through detachment.
Because he was already able to arise in this attainment with mastery at the moment of the first knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), it is said that he has "attained" it.
The merits of the Buddhas do not arise through preparatory effort (*prayoga*), because they manifest immediately according to their will.

If one is born among the non-conceptualizing beings (*asaṃjñisattva*) in the heavens, there exists a phenomenon that can cause the cessation of mind and mental factors; this is called "the state of non-conception" (*asaṃjñika*).

This is a truly existent entity; because it is the maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), it is called "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*) and is subsumed under the category of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Specifically, within the Heaven of Vast Results (*bṛhatphala*), there is a superior abode which, like the intermediate dhyāna, is named the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñi-deva*). It receives the name "non-conception" because while beings possess both mind and mental factors at the time of birth and at the time of death, these are absent during the intervening period.

When he is about to die, it is like one who has long been asleep awakening and giving rise to the thought of rising; having risen, he passes away before long and is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
One who is about to be born there must necessarily possess karma conducive to the subsequent life in the desire realm, as this is a determinate (*niyata*) karma.

Just as one who is about to be born in Uttarakuru must necessarily possess karma capable of inducing birth in the heavens, so too there is a causal continuity of the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) projected by prior karma that remains uninterrupted;
based upon this, the four modes of birth (catur-yoni) and five destinies (pañca-gati) are designated. This is called the life-faculty (jīvitendriya), and it is also termed lifespan (āyus).
Therefore, the Abhidharma says:
"What is the life-faculty?
It is the lifespan of the three realms."
This possesses substantial reality and is able to sustain warmth and consciousness,
as a verse says:
"When life, warmth, and consciousness— these three factors— abandon the body,"
The discarded body lies prostrate, like a log devoid of thought or sensation.
The Sūtras also state:

"Once one has experienced the ripening [of karma], one is called a denizen of hell (nāraka)"; it should be understood that this applies likewise up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
If there were no distinct phenomenon apart from the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) that is subsumed under the nature of a faculty and pervades all three realms,
then the four modes of birth and five destinies could not be established based upon it during the uninterrupted continuity of a single lifetime.

When one born in the formless realm gives rise to a wholesome or defiled mind of one’s own level or a higher level, or gives rise to an untainted mind of a lower level, upon what basis is this designated? Furthermore, when a being born by transformation in the heavenly realms gives rise to a wholesome or defiled mind, it should be called "death"; if they give rise to an indeterminate mind, it should again be called "birth."
To deny the existence of the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) would entail this great error.
That which causes various classes of sentient beings to perform similar activities and share similar inclinations is called the homogeneous character (nikāyasabhāga).
This, moreover, is of two kinds:
First, non-differentiation;
second, differentiation.
Regarding non-differentiation: it means that all sentient beings possess self-love, equally rely upon food, and share similar desires and inclinations.
This cause of equality is called the "homogeneity of beings" (*nikāya-sabhāga*); within each individual body, there is one distinct instance of it.

As for its distinctions, these refer to the various categories of sentient beings, such as differences in realm, level, destiny, mode of birth, lineage, gender, lay follower, monk, trainee, and non-trainee.
Within each individual body, there exists a cause consisting of the determination of shared karma, aspirations, and activities, which is termed the "homogeneous character" (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
If this did not exist, conventional designations such as "noble ones" and "non-noble ones" would all fall into confusion.
What is the difference between the state of being a worldling (*pṛthagjanatva*) and the commonality of worldlings (*pṛthagjanasabhāgatā*)?
That which serves as the cause for shared inclinations and so forth is called "that commonality" (*tatsabhāga*).
The state of being a worldling, however, is that which acts as the cause for all that is disadvantageous.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Bhikṣus, you should know: I say that for the foolish, unlearned worldling, there is not even the slightest evil or unwholesome karma that they are incapable of creating."
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
"If one comes among humans and attains the human *nikāya-sabhāga*, there is the sense of relinquishing and acquiring the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) at the time of death and birth.
Therefore, the nature of an ordinary person is distinct from the *nikāya-sabhāga*.

When all phenomena arise, there is an internal causal force that enables them to acquire their respective specific functions; this internal cause is designated as the "characteristic of arising" (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*).
Thus, there are generally two kinds of causes for the arising of phenomena:
first, the internal; [second, the external].
Second, the external.
"Internal" refers to the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*); "external" refers to the nature of the six causes or four conditions.

If the characteristic of arising were absent, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) would be like space and so forth; even though they possessed external causes and conditions, they would lack the meaning of arising.
Alternatively, it would follow that space and so forth also possess the property of being produced and thus have the nature of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);
this would be a great error.
Therefore, one knows that there exists a distinct characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*).
The cause that draws forth a distinct effect and enables temporary duration is called the characteristic of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*).

This means that when conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) abide for a brief period, each possesses a specific power capable of drawing forth a distinct effect to maintain that temporary duration.
The internal cause, which possesses the power to project a distinct effect, is called the characteristic of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*).
If this characteristic of duration did not exist, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) would be unable to project a distinct effect even during their momentary state of abiding.
From this, it is known that there exists a distinct characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*).
"Aging" (*jarā*) refers to the impairment of the capacity to project a result, rendering it unable to repeatedly project further results.
For if conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) lacked the characteristic of change (*anyathātva-lakṣaṇa*) to impair their capacity, for what reason would they be unable to project further results?
Since it has already been further cited, to cite it again and again would lead to an infinite regress.
If that were the case, it would also follow that it is not momentary (*kṣaṇika*).
Therefore, one knows that there exists a distinct characteristic of difference (*anyathātva-lakṣaṇa*).
Impermanence refers to that which, having impaired functional capacity, causes a present dharma to enter the past.
This means there is a distinct dharma called the "characteristic of cessation" (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*), which causes [dharmas] to fall from the present into the past.
If these did not exist, phenomena would not be subject to cessation, or else even space and so forth would possess the quality of cessation.
These four are the conditioned characteristics of the conditioned.
If these four conditioned characteristics are present, it is designated as "conditioned," and not as space and so forth.
Nevertheless, the Blessed One said:

"There are three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned; the arising of the conditioned can be known, as can its passing away and its alteration while abiding," because he wished for those beings to be trained to develop weariness toward the conditioned.

Just as it is shown that Kālī and Śrī dwell together, these two distinct characteristics are spoken of as one; therefore, there are definitely four conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*), which are not identical to the essence of the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) they characterize.

If the characterized entity were identical to the conditioned nature itself, then just as the characterized entity and its characteristics would be one, the characteristics themselves would also be mutually indistinguishable.

If that were so, then at the time of cessation, all phenomena would have to arise; at the time of arising, they would have to cease; or else they would never arise at all, because these four primary characteristics are themselves conditioned.
Just as the primary characteristics have four secondary characteristics— namely, birth-of-birth up to cessation-of-cessation—
they do not lead to an infinite regress, because while each of the four primary characteristics applies to eight phenomena, each secondary characteristic can only apply to one.

This means that when a dharma arises, nine dharmas arise together with its own self-substance: the self-substance constitutes one, while the primary characteristics (lakṣaṇa) and secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇa) constitute eight. Within these primary characteristics, the characteristic of arising (jāti-lakṣaṇa), excluding its own self-substance, gives rise to the remaining eight dharmas.
Among the nine dharmas produced within the secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*), only the primary production (*jāti*) arises, because its power is inferior.
It should be understood that the same applies to duration (*sthiti*), change (*jarā*), and cessation (*anityatā*).
The primary characteristics depend upon the dharma; the secondary characteristics depend upon the primary characteristics.

Because the dharma exists by virtue of its characteristics (lakṣaṇa), it possesses a causal activity; because the characteristics exist by virtue of their secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇa), they possess functional activity.
What is this functional activity?
It refers to arising, abiding, change, and cessation.
Regarding "that which is produced" and so forth, this refers to the capacity to project a fruit.
Therefore, although the substance (*svabhāva*) of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) exists eternally, its function (*kāritra*) is not constant;
for it is by means of these four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the power of internal and external causes that the function is established.

Regarding "the collection of names (nāmakāya), the collection of phrases (padakāya), and the collection of phonemes (vyañjanakāya)," these arise based on speech, appearing like the images of objects carried by cognition.
That which expresses its own meaning is called a name, a phrase, or a phoneme.
This is another designation for the chapter on "conception" (*saṃjñā*).

Just as visual consciousness and the like arise based on the eye and other faculties, appearing while bearing the images of objects such as forms, so too does [the mind] that cognizes its own object, such as names, function in the same way.

It is not the case that the vocal sound itself can directly express meaning; otherwise, when one speaks the word "fire," it would burn one's mouth. Rather, it is by depending upon speech that names such as "fire" arise, and it is through these names for fire and so forth that the objects fire and so forth are expressed.

"Expression" (abhilāpa) refers to that which can produce cognitive awareness in others regarding the meaning being manifested; it does not, however, "conjoin" with the object, because sound is subject to obstruction.
Furthermore, the position held by various commentators—that sound is eternal—is logically untenable.
One should not maintain that there exists a separate dharma, apart from these three—names, phrases, and syllables—that can express meaning.
However, four types of phenomena appear to share a single characteristic:
first, sound;
Second, names;
third, meanings;
fourth, knowledge.
In this context, "name" (*nāman*) refers to the conceptualization of form (*rūpa*) and so forth.

"Phrase" (*pada*) refers to that which brings the expression of meaning to completion; for example, the verse beginning with "Commit no evil," or as it is said in the world: "Devadatta drives the white oxen here to milk them."
"Phonemes" (*vyañjana*) refer to characters such as *a*, *i*, and so forth.
These three are each distinct; when combined, those of the same class are termed a "body" (*kāya*).
As the Great Sage has said:

"O Bhikṣus, you should know that when a Tathāgata appears in the world, there are the collections of names (nāmakāya), phrases (padakāya), and phonemes (vyañjanakāya) that can be understood; this refers to the collections of names, phrases, and phonemes for such dharmas as the truths, the aggregates, the bases, the elements, the fruits of śrāmaṇya, and dependent origination."

Furthermore, when the Blessed One says that the Tathāgata attains various sets of names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*), he intends to say that the Tathāgata attains those various sets of names, phrases, and phonemes belonging to the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).
"Et cetera" refers to the distinctions among these categories of meaning.
The meaning of the term "conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskāra*) should be understood as extending up to this point.
As for the meaning of the term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*): it is called consciousness because it generally discerns objects such as form and so forth.

That which arises with the assistance of the faculties such as the eye, performing its present function within the six types of objects such as form, and which merely performs a general discernment of the objective entities such as form, is designated as "consciousness."

If one can distinguish their specific characteristics, they are termed the mental factors (caitta), such as feeling (vedanā) and so forth; consciousness (vijñāna) lacks those functions and serves merely as their support.
The function of consciousness consists only in the act of discernment for a single moment within the present life; this too is called "mind" (manas) and is also called "consciousness" (citta).
It is also the provisional designation for the fundamental substance of sentient beings, having the function of discerning objects such as form.
Due to the distinctions among the faculties and their objects, it is said to be of six kinds, namely, from eye-consciousness up to mental consciousness.
The Buddha himself explained its characteristic in the sūtras, stating that it is designated as "consciousness" (vijñāna) because it is capable of discerning.
From this, one knows that discernment is its characteristic.
Previously, while examining the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta), it was stated that there are generally two kinds of causes for the arising of dharmas:
First, the internal;
second, the external.
The internal refers to the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*); the external refers to the nature of the six causes or the four conditions (*pratyaya*).
Now, one should investigate what the causes and conditions are.
There are six kinds of causes:
first, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).
2. Simultaneous cause;
3. Homogeneous cause; 4. Pervasive cause;
5. The ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*);
6. The efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
Mental states and mental factors that are mutually associated and apprehend a single object together are called the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).

Just as the mind is [the cause] for feeling and so forth, feeling and so forth are [the cause] for feeling and so forth, and feeling and so forth are again [the cause] for the mind— each excluding its own self-nature—
all conditioned phenomena that are mutually causes for one another, or share a single fruit, are called simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Just as the primary elements (mahābhūta) are related as the characterized and the characterizer, so too are the mind and its concomitants mutually related.
As for the distinction between the two types of causes: it is like merchants who, by lending mutual assistance, are able to traverse a perilous road; this is the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu).
All things that are consumed through food and drink share a common purpose; this is the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).

Regarding those factors that follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*), these refer to all mental concomitants (*caitta*), the meditative attainments (*dhyāna*), the untainted restraints (*anāsrava-saṃvara*), and the conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*). Because they fall together with the mind into the same time period, arise together, abide together, cease together, share the same fruit, share the same outflow (*niṣyanda*), share the same maturation (*vipāka*), and are caused by the same wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate [state], they are called "factors following the mind" by virtue of these ten causes.
All previously arisen dharmas of their own stage and their own category act as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for subsequent similar dharmas, just like seeds.
All previously arisen universal dharmas (*sarvatraga-dharma*) of their own stage act as pervasive causes (*sarvatraga-hetu*) for subsequent defiled dharmas.
All unwholesome dharmas and all wholesome dharmas associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) serve as ripening causes (*vipāka-hetu*) for their own respective ripened effects.

When any dharmas arise, with the exception of their own self-nature (*svabhāva*), all other dharmas serve as efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*), either by merely not obstructing them or by being able to produce them.

Regarding these six causes, they generally take all conditioned phenomena as their produced effects; that is to say, the associated cause and the coexistent cause obtain the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
Because that [result] arises by the power of this [cause], this is called *puruṣakāra* (human effort), and that is called the result (*phala*).

The similar-cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive-cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) obtain the result of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*). It is called "equal" (*sama*) because the result resembles the cause; it is called "outflow" (*niṣyanda*) because it flows forth from the cause. Thus, the result which is an outflow is termed the "result of outflow."

The ripening cause (vipāka-hetu) attains the ripening fruit (vipāka-phala). It is called "different" (vi-) because the fruit does not resemble its cause; "ripening" (pāka) refers to maturation in the sense of being fit for experience. Thus, the fruit that is itself the ripening is termed the "ripening fruit. It is comprised solely within the category of sentient beings and is of an unobscured-neutral nature (anivṛta-avyākṛta).
The efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu) obtains the dominant fruit (adhipati-phala), because by means of this dominant power, that [effect] is able to arise.

This is like the relationship between the eye-faculty and visual consciousness, or between farmers and the harvest; since subsequent phenomena arise due to the prior dominant influence, the fruit of such dominance is called the dominant fruit.

Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), is called the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*). This is obtained by means of the Path and is not produced by the Path; since the fruit is itself disjunction, it is termed the "fruit of disjunction.

There are four kinds of conditions (*pratyaya*): namely, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediately antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Excluding the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), the remaining five causes are termed the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Past and present mental states and their concomitants (*citta-caitta-dharma*), with the exception of the final mind and its concomitants of an Arhat, are termed the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
All phenomena are termed the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
The nature of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) is termed the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

That which can accommodate obstructive matter is the characteristic of space (*ākāśa*); because it arises through the power of this dominance, and because its nature is that of space, it is able to provide accommodation.
If this [space] did not exist, obstructed objects would be unable to arise, as there would be no room for them.
As the Blessed One said:
"Brahmin, you should know that wind depends upon space."
The brahmin asked:
"Upon what does space depend?
The Buddha replied again:
Your question is unreasonable.
Space is colorless, invisible, and non-obstructive; on what could it possibly depend? Nevertheless, because there is light, space can be discerned.
Therefore, one knows that the unconditioned entity of space truly exists.
If this substance did not exist, upon what would the wind depend and abide?
If one says that form and so forth do not exist, upon what would such words rely?
Since there is light, what is it that is discerned?
This is because [the cessation] of things such as tortoise hair is not due to this [path].
The permanent severance of all suffering is called "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What is meant by "all suffering"?
This refers to all births and deaths.
As the Blessed One said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that whatever exists as becoming is itself called suffering; 'becoming' is merely another name for birth and death."

If there is non-arising, it is called the eternal cessation of suffering; like a dam holding back water or a wall blocking the wind, that which prevents suffering from arising is termed "cessation through discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
"Discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā*) means to select and discriminate; it is a preeminent, virtuous wisdom.
The cessation attained through the repeated discernment of the Four Noble Truths is designated as "cessation through discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This [cessation] is infinite in its substantiality according to what is abandoned, because the phenomena to be abandoned are limitless in number.
If their essence were one, then since the first path would have already attained it, the cultivation of subsequent paths would be rendered useless.

If you say that what was initially realized was only a partial portion and not the whole, then a single essence of cessation would necessarily possess multiple parts; however, for a single essence to have multiple parts contradicts logical principle.
Just as there is a certain measure of contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*), one should know that the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is likewise.
This explanation is excellent, for it accords with correct principle.

According to the distinctions among the paths, eighty-nine [types] are established; according to the abandonments of full knowledge (*parijñā*), nine types are established; and according to the five categories (*pañcavarga*), five types are established.
Furthermore, based on the distinctions among the fruits, they are collectively established as four, namely, the Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) and so forth.
Based on the distinctions among the realms of abandonment, detachment, and cessation, three are established.

Based on the distinctions between the abandonment of suffering and its origin, the presence of a remainder of support (*sopadhiśeṣa*), and the absence of a remainder of support (*nirupadhiśeṣa*), two types are collectively established; and with respect to the total abandonment of birth and death, one is collectively established.
Thus, this analytical cessation has many synonyms, namely: exhaustion (*kṣaya*), detachment (*virāga*), cessation (*nirodha*), nirvāṇa, and so forth.
As it is said in the *Pudgala-sūtra*:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that the four formless aggregates, together with the eye, visible objects, and so on, are collectively termed a 'person' (*pudgala*). Within this, one speaks metaphorically of a 'sentient being' (*sattva*), also called 'mind-born' (*manomaya*), and also called a 'person,' a 'mānava,' and so forth."

In this context, one refers to oneself as "I" and speaks of the eyes and so forth seeing forms and so forth, giving rise to various conventional discourses such as: "This venerable one has such a name, such a clan," and so on, as explained at length.
"O bhikṣus, you should know that these are merely conceptualizations and merely verbal designations; all such phenomena are impermanent.
Being conditioned and dependently originated, they are therefore suffering—namely, suffering at the time of arising, and suffering likewise during their duration and so forth."

In this regard, the permanent cessation without remainder of all these sufferings—their removal, abandonment, transformation, vomiting out, exhaustion, detachment from passion, extinction, pacification, and disappearance—such that they do not continue to arise again, is called "permanent non-arising."
This is the ultimate tranquility and excellence, namely: the relinquishing of all bases, the exhaustion of craving, detachment, cessation, and nirvāṇa.
As for what is called "the relinquishing of all bases," it means that within this cessation, one forever abandons the suffering of all five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
Regarding the term "exhaustion of craving" (*tṛṣṇākṣaya*): it means that within this cessation, all cravings are currently exhausted.
Having attained this cessation, one is forever separated from defiled phenomena; therefore, it is called "separation" (*virāga*).
Having realized this cessation, all sufferings are stilled; therefore, it is called "cessation" (*nirodha*).
Having realized this cessation, all calamities and the fires of the afflictions (*kleśa*) are extinguished; therefore, it is called *nirvāṇa*.

As for "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it refers to a distinct dharma that absolutely obstructs the arising of future dharmas; it occurs solely due to the deficiency of conditions and is not obtained through deliberation.
For example, when the eye and the mind are focused exclusively on a single form, other forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles pass away.

Because the five groups of consciousness and so forth that take those objects as their conditions have attained this cessation—which serves as a permanent obstruction—they abide in the future and will never arise again.
Because the absence of conditions also arises from the power of cessation, non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is definitely a real entity.
As the Blessed One said:
"If at that time a pleasant feeling is present, the other two feelings then cease."
As for that which is called "cessation," what else could it be?
It is certainly neither impermanence nor analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Furthermore, the Sūtra says:

"O Bhikṣus, you should know that if one has attained the stage of Stream-enterer (srotāpanna), one has already exhausted the hells, exhausted the realm of hungry ghosts (preta), and exhausted the animal realm (tiryagyoni).

This term 'exhausted' refers to non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha); for at that time, the dharmas of karmic maturation (vipāka) have not yet attained analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha)."
For the sake of beginners who delight in diligent study, this treatise has been briefly composed, setting aside various questions and answers.

Those who have not fully understood the profound and subtle characteristics of the Abhidharma will, according to their own whims, assemble a mass of frivolous arguments and place them before them; they falsely construct perverse objections with the intent to revile [the teaching], thereby slandering the supreme instruction spoken by the Buddha.
As the World-Honored One has said:

there are two kinds of people who slander the Buddha’s sublime teaching; first, those who lack faith and give rise to hatred and envy; second, those who, though they have faith, receive and uphold [the teaching] with aversion.
The Abhidharmāvatāra-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School, Volume II.
